T3.title: Classifying IDEs
T3.accept:
In the list of IDEs from the previous question, you can find lightweight and heavyweight IDEs. 

Lightweight IDEs are basically text editors enhanced with features for writing code (e.g., highlighting, completion, compiling, etc.) 

Heavyweight IDEs offer a more complete set of features, which may include tools to simplify the construction of graphical user interfaces, integration with database systems, version control systems, and deployment environments, tools for team collaboration, class and object browsers, etc. 

How would you classify the list above in these two categories? If you are not familiar with a specific IDE, conduct some light research about it.

T4.title: Using GitHub Issue Tracker
T4.accept:
PART II - ISSUE TRACKERS

Let's use an issue tracker. Create a new repository on GitHub titled ‘cs386-a2.1’ (only one for the group) and add your teammates as collaborators (you can do this in the ‘settings’ section). If a teammate does not have a GitHub account, assist them in setting one up. If you are working individually, add the instructor to your repository (you can find the instructor's GitHub ID on the “About the Teaching Staff” page in the “Start Here” module on Canvas). 

Imagine that your team is developing software for a self-driving car. Each group member should create 2 issues that read like new feature requests and 2 that read like bug fix requests (be creative, we should be able to infer from the title whether the issue is a feature or a bug). 

Paste here a screenshot of the issue tracker showing the list of issues.

T11.title: Mentioning developers
T11.accept: Sometimes, you may want the opinion of a teammate about the issue you are working on. You can mention a teammate using the @ symbol in a comment, and they will be notified. If you are working individually, mention the instructor. Paste a screenshot here showing the mention of one of the issues (one example is sufficient).

T12.title: Linking issues
T12.accept: Often, issues are interrelated, and you want to connect them. Each teammate should refer to another issue in a comment using the "#" symbol followed by the issue number (e.g., "I think the problem started in #45", "this should be fixed after #32", etc.). When you do this, GitHub creates an event in the referred issue. Paste here a screenshot showing an example of an issue referencing another one.

T15.title: Markdown language
T15.accept:
PART III - DOCUMENTATION TOOLS

Let's create a Readme file for your project. GitHub adopts a markdown notation (https://guides.github.com/features/mastering-markdown/). Create a new file named readme.md in your repository (‘Code’ tab on GitHub) and write Markdown code to produce an output similar to the following figure, following the provided instructions. 

![Unit 2 Tooling Overview](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=view&id=1aVpe0ADqL3NM8dMBjPzUsoKYrT1PWYi3)

Requirements:
MyCarDriver should be a first-level heading.
Installation and Developers should be second-level headings.
The term pip should be linked to https://pypi.org/project/pip/ 
The pip logo should come from this URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/explore/666de02829613e0244e9441b114edb85781e972c/topics/pip/pip.png
